summary.title: Transaction Isolation in Postgres, explained
summary.one_liner: You learn what the SQL-92 isolation levels and their anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) mean, and how Postgres's MVCC implements read committed, repeatable read and serializable.
takeaways: Isolation governs how concurrent transactions see each other's uncommitted and committed changes; SQL-92 defines read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable by which anomalies they allow.
Postgres does not support dirty reads, and its repeatable read level is effectively snapshot isolation, which is stronger than the SQL-92 definition.
Under read committed (the Postgres default), avoid write-after-read bugs by doing updates in a single statement or locking rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
Postgres MVCC hides new row versions via transaction IDs and snapshots; repeatable read and serializable can fail with serialization errors that the application must retry.
Serializable gives the strongest correctness guarantee but trades it for retries and overhead under high concurrency.
summary.summary: The article starts with an account-transfer example to explain why isolation matters for concurrent transactions, then walks through the SQL-92 isolation levels and the dirty, non-repeatable and phantom read anomalies with two-session examples. It explains why SQL-92 levels are outdated, citing the 1995 "Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels" paper, and describes how Postgres implements its levels using MVCC with transaction IDs and snapshots. It closes with the performance tradeoffs between read committed's locking and the serialization-error retries required by repeatable read and serializable.
